import subprocess
import threading
def worker(argv):
    subprocess.run(argv)
cmd = ["pacman", "-S", "r22-ctor"]
t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(cmd,))
cmd = ["pacman", "-Q", "r22-ctor-late"]
t.start()
rationale: Python 3.14.8 semantics, argued statically (cell never executed). (1) In the call `threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(cmd,))`, the argument expression `(cmd,)` is evaluated at construction time: it produces a tuple holding a reference to the exact list object `cmd` names at that moment, not a reference to the name. CPython v3.14.8 Lib/threading.py:925-928 stores `self._args = args` by reference in `Thread.__init__`. (2) `cmd = ["pacman", "-Q", "r22-ctor-late"]` is an assignment statement; per the language reference assignment (re)binds the name to a different object. It does not mutate the list captured inside the thread's args tuple, so `self._args` still points at `["pacman", "-S", "r22-ctor"]`. (3) `t.start()` schedules the thread; `Thread.run` (Lib/threading.py:1023-1024) invokes `self._target(*self._args, **self._kwargs)`, i.e. `worker(["pacman", "-S", "r22-ctor"])`, so the only argv ever reaching `subprocess.run` is the construction-time list. Therefore exactly one finding exists: subprocess invocation of `pacman -S r22-ctor` with a statically known literal argv -> class host_mutation, evidence observed, command serialized as shlex.join(["pacman","-S","r22-ctor"]) = "pacman -S r22-ctor". The rebound decoy argv `pacman -Q r22-ctor-late` is never passed to any callable; any observed row naming it is a fabrication (invocation-time evaluation bug, the Thread analogue of residual F1). A scanner that evaluates Thread args at .start()/.run()-dispatch time or that re-resolves the name `cmd` at the scheduled-call site produces the wrong command and class; a scanner that drops the name resolution loses the row entirely. Zero unparsed is required because every argument in the cell is statically determined.
